Legendary coach Frank Girardi honored as Girardi Stadium hosts its first game

Prior to Lycoming's debut home game at Girardi Stadium, it hosted a pregame ceremony to honor the legendary coach. Fifteen years after his retirement, the university had announced it would be renaming its football stadium and on Saturday, it was set to play its first home contest with that in effect.

After being introduced by his son, Jerry, Frank Girardi gave a two-minute speech of his own.

When he was finished, he received strong ovations from the crowd of fans gathered in the stands and the one of alumni and former players standing behind him. It was clear that the community still supported Girardi tremendously.

"That was awesome. I love Coach Girardi and I love all the guys that have played here," said Lycoming coach Mike Clark on watching Girardi be honored today. "Coach Girardi absolutely, positively deserves the honor that he got here today. It was really cool to see this happen for him."

Throughout his speech, he offered endless thanks.

From President Kent Trachte and the Board of Trustees for granting him the honor, to his players and coaches for helping him guide the program to meteoric success, to the university and community for all the opportunities and support they provided for him and his family, he held endless gratitude for all that Lycoming College have given him throughout the decades.

"The best part of achieving any recognition that you may receive in your lifetime is sharing it with others," said Girardi during his speech. "Your family, your loved ones, your friends, the outstanding fans that we have. And that's what I'm doing today. I'm sharing this wonderful day with all of you."

Throughout his time as the head coach of the football team, he led the Warriors to 257 wins – tenth in Division III football, 11 playoff appearances, two trips to the Stagg Bowl and 13 conference titles, cementing himself not just in Lycoming football history but NCAA football history. Along with being inducted into the Lycoming Athletics and State of Pennsylvania Hall of Fames, he was inducted into the College Football Hall of Fame in 2016.

Warri Wolves recorded their first win of the 2019/2020 Nigeria Professional Football League, NPFL, on Sunday, November 17 in their Matchday 3 fixture against Adamawa United.

In the opening quarter of the game, Warri Wolves enjoyed more of ball possession but found it hard to thread through the desired passes in the final third.

However, fortunes of the home team improved midway in the first half, as they created scoring chances to go ahead in the tie.

But Adamawa United goalie, Pwadadi Bulus, stood firm between the sticks and thwarted several scoring efforts.

The halftime pep talks put Warri Wolves on the front foot, as they frantically went in search of goals.

At the end of the match, an elated Evans Ogenyi, technical adviser of Warri Wolves, said he was happy with the outcome of the encounter.

Though he acknowledged that the team missed some scoring opportunities in the opening half, Ogenyi commended his side for their improved performance in the second stanza of the fixture.

"I'm happy with the result," said Ogenyi." This is the kind of result we had wanted before now."

"We missed some of our opportunities to score in the first half. But we came into the game later and we got the result we want. I praise the boys for playing according to what we noted at halftime."

A new dawn was upon the Premier League before the 2013/14 season started. The competition was without the most successful manager in British football history for the first time after Sir Alex Ferguson retired from his post at Manchester United, with David Moyes taking the helm.

Our Old Trafford stadium, commonly known as "The Theatre of Dreams," was originally opened on February 19, 1910 with a capacity of approximately 80,000. During the Second World War, Old Trafford was used by the military as a depot, and on March 11, 1941 was heavily damaged by a German bombing raid. The stadium was rebuilt following the war and reopened on August 24, 1949. The addition of floodlighting, permitting evening matches, was completed in 1957 and a project to cover the stands with roofs was completed in 1959. After a series of additions during the 1960s, 1970s and early 1980s, capacity at Old Trafford reached 56,385 in 1985. The conversion of the stadium to an all-seater reduced capacity to approximately 44,000 by 1992, the lowest in its history. Thereafter, we began to expand capacity throughout the stadium, bringing capacity to approximately 58,000 by 1996, approximately 68,000 by 2000, and approximately 76,000 in 2006.
